doc.title: Dave Bailey and John McNeil Interview, 1959-10-25

chapter: Young Tuxedo and Chris Kelly years
title: Trumpeter Walter Blue collapses and dies at a parade
summary: Bailey tells how Blue, playing hard in a hot parade, fell ill and died within fifteen minutes; he recalls the tomb.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: That fellow that I told you. He dropped there with us. He didn't drop there. He dropped dead from playing a parade up with the- No, but I'll tell you how it was. Was that Washington? When I was in the car, he was in the car.
He was in the car. He dropped dead from playing a parade up with the-

No, but I'll tell you how it was. Was that Washington? Was that Washington? Fourth and- Let me see, not Fourth. Sixth and St. Thomas. That's where the band was supposed to meet. It was in the summertime. Hot. We were all that on white shirts and black ties and things. And I don't forget what time it was we were supposed to leave there. He was rather late. And so when he came, so when he came, when he came there, he was late. And Brown, Chris Kelly was playing with Brown Band then. And this little fella called, let me see his drum player's name. I can't think of this little drum player's name. Sun White. Sun White, do you know Sun White? Yeah, his name is Edmund Washington.
I bet you didn't know that.

That's his real name. No, I didn't know it. Sun White. Well he live up on Long Street now, I believe. Back real quick. He was playing with them. I said, watch out, Blue. I said, Brown and Kelly's banger runs in today. You know what he said? He said, well, I'm going to toot this trumpet today. Brown and Kelly's nobody. I said, man, he cuddled us on the drum. We left him there and went down the fourth seat. It was hot that day, Fulton Thomas. We got a beer. It was all rain and wet. This from 6th Street to Fulton Thomas. That's how hot it was, rain and wet. So we went back, come back up and went back to Washington Street. And when I got to Magazine Street, he comes and starts playing the snare drum. And I don't forget who was playing the bass drum. And he kept on coming back on me and I told him to say, Walter Blue. That's Walter Blue you're talking.
Yeah, Walter Blue, yes. Yeah, I know who you're talking about.
Yeah. He says, and his son, he got a son, every time his son sees me, his son started crying. His son is working at Lutchen's now.

Every time his son sees me, his son, they're boiling, they drink, they see me, he started telling people about me and they started crying. About my dad. Every time I see him, it's a damn thing with my dad. And when we got most of the camp street, after we crossed Magazine, after Magazine is camp, he said, come on, let's play a number now. And the band started off, that man went way up above the steps, like Lou's what I said. And I said, I ain't never heard him blow like that before. And as soon as we got most of the grade, most of the college team, he got out to the parade. And look, he done this. And he ran to the gutter and he stuck his finger and everything like that. And I told my brother and I said, you all better stop us, that man's sick. Grandma and my brother said, oh come on, he's all right. I said, that man is sick. He said, let's stop. That man bad off. And when he vomited, he vomited. It was black paint, charcoal, and he vomited. And there's a no-called man later, a little iron picket pen. And he ran in there, tried to get assistance from there. Just that quick man. And he ran in there. And we had them went all the way to Pachanga. The police come back on horse, the police on horseback. Come back, and a colored woman with a little white bear like you know, a colored woman letting the white baby down. Run with the little drum. And I got there and fell flat on that pavement. He hid that pavement. And they picked him up, put him on the gyar. We had a mouth full of gold, diamond rings, pins, watch. Lately these nice looking fellas, you know. Bright fun. Had a hair like white boy, like y'all. Lately him up on the gyar and put a pill on his head. And we got there and he was just always saying, hmm. And they sent him to the hospital. Fifteen minutes after he got in the hospital in his day. That's right. And after that, after we played that parade, it got dark just like night. And when we got to the drive in Jackson, it was in the water up there. It was right in the thunder and lightning. Yeah. And I think about him a lot of times. And I know the tomb that he's buried in. And every time I pass on a Louisiana bus, I'm like I'm going to go to my barber first and I look at that tomb. He was a teamster, you know. And they put him in that tomb. And I look at that tomb. And every time his son see me, he'd cry.
Where is that tomb exactly? I like to see it.

It's a tomb just as you cross. Seventh Street. It's the second big tomb on this side. Right at the front. It's not the first one this way, but the one going to Washington. The first big tomb. I try to look at that. Shake my head. And I say, you know, I look at them gray. I say, I don't see how people can be so mean, white and colored, and always take one another life. You know, it's a sad thing, you know. To see how we got to leave here and never come back no more, you know. It is. It's sad.
I couldn't do that. I didn't do that. Is Blue's name on that tomb?

It might be. I don't know. I didn't. I'll ask his son. I'm so excited. But he's wasn't. I'll ask Young Blue. Hmm? It's been a long time. Because my first wife died in 1923. I was living on that. Where'd you get it? She was living when he died in 1923. And she was 29 years old when she died. And you know how old she would be now. In 1923. She's from Rhode Island, Louisiana. I shipped her by the way. I was a bearer. And that's when the time he died. But his real name is Walter Donison.
